cards.q: State the main observations of Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment, and what each shows about the atom.
cards.a: Most alpha particles go straight through; a tiny number bounce back.
marks: Most alpha particles pass straight through the foil: the atom is mostly empty space.
A few are deflected through small angles: there is a concentration of positive charge that repels them.
A very few are deflected through more than 90°: the positive charge and most of the mass are in a tiny, dense nucleus.

cards.q: What is an alpha particle, and how far does it travel in air? What stops it?
cards.a: A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons, charge \(+2e\)). Its range in air is a few centimetres, and it is stopped by a sheet of paper.

cards.q: What is a beta-minus particle, and how far does it travel in air? What stops it?
cards.a: A fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus. Its range in air is about a metre, and it is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.

cards.q: What is gamma radiation, and what is needed to reduce its intensity?
cards.a: High-frequency electromagnetic radiation (photons) from the nucleus. It is never fully stopped: several centimetres of lead, or metres of concrete, reduce its intensity greatly.

cards.q: Explain why alpha radiation is the most ionising of the three types, yet has the shortest range.
cards.a: It loses its energy quickly because it ionises so heavily.
marks: An alpha particle has a large charge and moves relatively slowly, so it ionises many atoms along its path.
Each ionisation takes energy from the alpha particle.
It therefore loses all its kinetic energy in a short distance.

cards.q: Outline how absorbers can be used to identify the type of radiation a source emits.
cards.a: Place absorbers between the source and a detector, one at a time, and see which reduces the count rate.
marks: Measure the background count rate with no source, and subtract it from every later reading.
Place the source a fixed distance from a Geiger–Müller tube and record the count rate.
Insert paper: a large drop in count rate shows alpha.
Insert a few millimetres of aluminium: a large drop shows beta.
If a count above background remains that only thick lead reduces, the source emits gamma.

cards.q: Which type of radiation is used to monitor the thickness of aluminium foil or paper during manufacture, and why not alpha or gamma?
cards.a: Beta. Alpha would be stopped completely by the sheet, and gamma would pass through almost unaffected, so neither would show small changes in thickness.
cards.why: Gamma is used for thick steel, where beta would be absorbed completely.

cards.q: Why is an alpha source far more dangerous inside the body than outside it?
cards.a: Outside, alpha particles are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin. Inside, they are absorbed by living tissue, where their very strong ionising power does great damage to cells.

cards.q: State the inverse-square law for gamma radiation from a point source.
cards.a: The intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source: \(I = \frac{k}{x^{2}}\).

cards.q: The corrected count rate from a gamma source is 400 counts per second at 0.10 m. Calculate the corrected count rate at 0.20 m.
cards.a: 100 counts per second
steps: Intensity follows an inverse-square law, so it falls to \(\frac{1}{2^{2}} = \frac{1}{4}\).

cards.q: Outline how to verify the inverse-square law for gamma radiation.
cards.a: Measure the corrected count rate at a range of distances and plot it against \(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\).
marks: Measure the background count rate with the source well away, and subtract it from every reading.
Place the gamma source at a measured distance \(x\) from a Geiger–Müller tube and record the count over a fixed time.
Repeat for a range of distances, counting for long enough at each to get a large count.
Plot the corrected count rate against \(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\): a straight line through the origin confirms the law.

cards.q: Give three sources of background radiation.
cards.a: Radon gas and rocks in the ground, cosmic rays from space, and medical sources such as X-rays. Food and drink also contribute.

cards.q: A detector near a source records 132 counts per minute. With the source removed it records 12 counts per minute. What is the corrected count rate?
cards.a: 120 counts per minute
steps: The reading without the source is the background.

cards.q: Outline how to investigate the absorption of gamma radiation by lead.
cards.a: Measure the corrected count rate through increasing thicknesses of lead and plot a log graph.
marks: Measure the background count rate and subtract it from every reading.
Fix a gamma source and a Geiger–Müller tube a constant distance apart.
Place lead sheets of measured thickness between them and record the count rate for each total thickness.
Plot the natural log of the corrected count rate against thickness: a straight line shows that the absorption is exponential.

cards.q: State three precautions for handling a radioactive source safely in the laboratory.
cards.a: Handle it with long tongs to keep it at a distance, keep the exposure time short, and store it in a lead-lined container. Never point it at anyone.

cards.q: Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous. What does each word mean?
cards.a: Random: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next, or when a particular nucleus will decay. Spontaneous: the decay is not affected by outside conditions such as temperature or pressure.

cards.q: Define the decay constant.
cards.a: The probability that a given nucleus decays per unit time. Unit: \(\text{s}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Define the activity of a radioactive source, and state how it relates to the number of undecayed nuclei.
cards.a: The number of nuclei that decay per unit time. Unit: the becquerel, Bq. \(A = \lambda N\).

cards.q: Write the equation for the number of undecayed nuclei remaining after a time \(t\).
cards.a: \(N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}\)
cards.why: Activity follows the same form: \(A = A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}\).

cards.q: Define half-life.
cards.a: The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay. It is also the time for the activity to halve.

cards.q: Write the equation linking half-life to the decay constant.
cards.a: \(T_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\)

cards.q: An isotope has a half-life of 8.0 days. Calculate its decay constant in \(\text{s}^{-1}\).
cards.a: \(1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

cards.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq. What is its activity after three half-lives?
cards.a: 100 Bq
steps: The activity halves in each half-life.

cards.q: A sample contains \(5.0 \times 10^{15}\) undecayed nuclei of an isotope with decay constant \(1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). Calculate its activity.
cards.a: \(5.0 \times 10^{9}\ \text{Bq}\)

cards.q: An isotope has a half-life of 8.0 days. Calculate the fraction of a sample that remains undecayed after 20 days.
cards.a: 0.18
cards.why: The time and the half-life may both stay in days, as long as the units match.

cards.q: Calculate the number of nuclei in 1.0 g of cobalt-60. (molar mass \(60\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(N_{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(1.0 \times 10^{22}\)
cards.why: This is the usual first step when a question gives a mass and asks for an activity.

cards.q: For a radioactive source, what graph gives a straight line, and how is the decay constant found from it?
cards.a: \(\ln N\) (or \(\ln A\)) against \(t\). The gradient is \(-\lambda\).
cards.why: Taking logs of \(N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}\) gives \(\ln N = \ln N_{0} - \lambda t\).

cards.q: How is the half-life found from a graph of activity against time?
cards.a: Read off the time taken for the activity to fall to half of any starting value. Repeat for several starting values and take the mean.

cards.q: Explain the principle of radioactive carbon dating.
cards.a: Living things take in carbon-14 and keep a constant proportion of it. After death no more is taken in, and the carbon-14 decays with a known half-life. Measuring the fraction remaining gives the time since death.

cards.q: Why does the half-life of an isotope matter when deciding how to store radioactive waste?
cards.a: An isotope with a long half-life stays active for a very long time, so the waste must be kept isolated and secure for thousands of years.

cards.q: Describe the graph of neutron number \(N\) against proton number \(Z\) for stable nuclei.
cards.a: For light nuclei it follows the line \(N = Z\). For heavier nuclei it curves upwards: stable heavy nuclei have more neutrons than protons.
cards.why: Extra neutrons add to the strong attraction without adding to the electrostatic repulsion between protons.

cards.q: How does an unstable nucleus decay if it has too many neutrons, too many protons, or is simply too heavy?
cards.a: Too many neutrons: \(\beta^{-}\) decay. Too many protons: \(\beta^{+}\) decay or electron capture. Too heavy: alpha decay.

cards.q: State the changes in nucleon number and proton number for alpha, \(\beta^{-}\) and \(\beta^{+}\) decay.
cards.a: Alpha: nucleon number −4, proton number −2. \(\beta^{-}\): nucleon number unchanged, proton number +1. \(\beta^{+}\): nucleon number unchanged, proton number −1.
cards.why: Electron capture changes the numbers in the same way as \(\beta^{+}\) decay.

cards.q: Write the nuclear equation for the alpha decay of uranium-238, \({}^{238}_{92}\text{U}\), into thorium (Th).
cards.why: Check that both the top numbers and the bottom numbers balance.

cards.q: Why is gamma radiation often emitted after an alpha or beta decay, and how does it change the nucleus?
cards.a: The decay can leave the new nucleus in an excited state. It drops to a lower energy state by emitting a gamma photon. Neither the nucleon number nor the proton number changes.

cards.q: Give two reasons why technetium-99m is suitable as a tracer in medical diagnosis.
cards.a: It emits only gamma radiation, which passes out of the body to be detected and causes little ionisation inside it. Its half-life of about 6 hours is long enough for the scan but short enough that the dose soon falls.

cards.q: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 5.0 MeV is fired directly at a gold nucleus (proton number 79). Estimate its distance of closest approach. (\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\); \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(4.5 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{m}\)
steps: At closest approach all the kinetic energy has become electric potential energy: \(E_{k} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Qq}{r}\).
cards.why: This is an upper limit for the radius of the nucleus.

cards.q: Why does electron diffraction give a better value for nuclear radius than the closest approach of alpha particles?
cards.a: The alpha particle stops short of the nucleus, so its closest approach overestimates the radius, and alpha particles also feel the strong force. Electrons are leptons: they are not affected by the strong force and are diffracted by the nucleus itself.

cards.q: Describe the graph of intensity against angle for high-energy electrons diffracted by a nucleus.
cards.a: The intensity falls as the angle increases, with a minimum followed by a small rise. The angle of the first minimum is used to find the radius of the nucleus.

cards.q: Write the equation for how the radius of a nucleus depends on its nucleon number.
cards.a: \(R = R_{0}A^{\frac{1}{3}}\), where \(R_{0}\) is a constant, about 1.2 fm.

cards.q: Calculate the radius of a nucleus of nucleon number 64. (\(R_{0} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\))
cards.a: \(4.8 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\)

cards.q: Explain how \(R = R_{0}A^{\frac{1}{3}}\) shows that all nuclei have about the same density.
cards.a: It makes the volume proportional to the nucleon number, just as the mass is.
marks: The volume of a nucleus is \(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_{0}^{3}A\), so volume is proportional to \(A\).
The mass of a nucleus is also proportional to \(A\), the number of nucleons.
Density is mass ÷ volume, so \(A\) cancels: the density is the same for every nucleus.

cards.q: Estimate the density of nuclear matter. (nucleon mass \(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\); \(R_{0} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\))
cards.a: \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}\)
steps: Consider one nucleon (\(A = 1\)): its radius is \(R_{0}\).
cards.why: Enormously greater than the density of ordinary matter, because atoms are mostly empty space.

cards.q: What is the mass defect of a nucleus?
cards.a: The difference between the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons and the mass of the nucleus itself. The nucleus always has the smaller mass.

cards.q: Define the binding energy of a nucleus.
cards.a: The energy needed to separate the nucleus completely into its individual protons and neutrons. It is the energy equivalent of the mass defect.

cards.q: What is the atomic mass unit, and what energy is equivalent to 1 u?
cards.a: One twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom: \(1\ \text{u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\). It is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

cards.q: A helium-4 nucleus has a mass defect of 0.0304 u. Calculate its binding energy in MeV. (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
cards.a: 28.3 MeV
cards.why: That is about 7.1 MeV per nucleon.

cards.q: Describe the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number.
cards.a: It rises steeply for light nuclei, reaches a maximum near iron-56, then falls gradually for heavier nuclei.
cards.why: Nuclei near the peak are the most stable.

cards.q: Use the binding energy per nucleon curve to explain why both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei release energy.
cards.a: In both cases the products are closer to the peak of the curve, so they have a greater binding energy per nucleon. The increase in binding energy is released.
cards.why: Fusion moves light nuclei up the steep left side; fission moves heavy nuclei up the gentle right side.

cards.q: Explain why nuclear fusion needs a very high temperature and a very high density.
cards.a: The nuclei must get close enough for the strong force to act, and must collide often.
marks: Nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other electrostatically.
They must come within the very short range of the strong nuclear force to fuse.
A very high temperature gives the nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome the repulsion.
A very high density makes collisions frequent enough to keep the reaction going.

cards.q: In a fission reaction the total mass of the products is 0.200 u less than the mass of the reactants. Calculate the energy released in MeV. (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
cards.a: 186 MeV
steps: The lost mass has become energy.

cards.q: What is induced fission, and how can it lead to a chain reaction?
cards.a: A heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a slow (thermal) neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and two or three neutrons. Those neutrons can cause further fissions.

cards.q: What is meant by critical mass?
cards.a: The minimum mass of fuel needed for a chain reaction to keep going: on average one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another.
cards.why: In a smaller mass, too many neutrons escape through the surface.

cards.q: What is the function of the moderator in a thermal nuclear reactor? Name a suitable material.
cards.a: It slows the fast neutrons released by fission, through elastic collisions, so that they can be absorbed by more fuel nuclei. Water or graphite.
cards.why: The moderator's nuclei should be light: a neutron loses most energy colliding with a nucleus of similar mass.

cards.q: What is the function of the control rods in a nuclear reactor? Name a suitable material.
cards.a: They absorb neutrons, to control the rate of fission. Lowering them further absorbs more neutrons and slows the reaction. Boron or cadmium.

cards.q: A student writes: "The moderator absorbs neutrons to control the reaction." Correct this.
cards.a: The moderator slows neutrons down; it does not absorb them. It is the control rods that absorb neutrons to control the rate of the reaction.

cards.q: What is the function of the coolant in a nuclear reactor?
cards.a: It carries thermal energy away from the reactor core to a heat exchanger, where it is used to make steam to drive turbines.

cards.q: State three safety features of a nuclear reactor.
cards.a: Thick concrete shielding round the core to absorb radiation. Remote handling of fuel rods. An emergency shut-down system that drops the control rods fully into the core.

cards.q: How is high-level radioactive waste from a reactor dealt with?
cards.a: Spent fuel rods are handled remotely and first kept in cooling ponds for several years. The waste is then sealed, for example in glass inside steel containers, and stored securely deep underground.
